title: Diphthongs
subtitle: Au, ei, ey — two vowels, one syllable.
objectives: Pronounce the three main diphthongs: au, ei, ey.
Distinguish diphthongs from vowel sequences across syllable boundaries.

sections.heading: What is a diphthong
sections.body:
A diphthong is two vowels pronounced as one syllable. The tongue moves from one vowel position to another without a break. English has many: the i in ride (aɪ), the ow in how (aʊ), the oy in boy (ɔɪ).

Old Norse has three main diphthongs: au, ei, ey. Each is one syllable. The stress falls on the first element, and the tongue glides to the second.

sections.heading: Au
sections.body:
Au = [au], as in English house or cow. The vowel starts at [a] (father) and glides to [u] (put). Common words: auga (eye), daudi (death), lauss (loose), haugr (mound).

Do not confuse au with a + u across a syllable boundary. In the word fara + -um (we go), the a and u are separate syllables: fa-rum. In daudi, au is one syllable: dau-di.

sections.heading: Ei
sections.body:
Ei = [ei], as in English bay or say. The vowel starts at [e] (met) and glides to [i] (machine). Common words: ein (one), einn (alone), heimr (world, home), steinn (stone).

This is the most common diphthong in Old Norse. You will see it everywhere.

sections.heading: Ey
sections.body:
Ey = [øy]. The first element is ø (mid front rounded, as in French peu), the second is y (high front rounded, as in French tu). English has no equivalent. To approximate: say the ay in say, round your lips, then glide upward toward ee with lips still rounded.

Common words: ey (island), eyra (ear), deyja (to die).

sections.heading: Ǫu (rare)
sections.body: Ǫu appears in a handful of words. It is [ɔu] — the vowel of caught gliding to the vowel of put. Rare enough that some grammars do not list it as a phoneme, but you will see it: jǫtunn (giant), sometimes spelled with ǫu in older texts.

sections.heading: Listening drill
sections.instructions: Each diphthong is spoken in isolation, then in three words. Repeat aloud.

items.answer: Like English house — starts at [a], glides to [u].
Like English bay — starts at [e], glides to [i].
Like ay in say, but with rounded lips throughout. Glides from ø to y.

items.prompt: Is au in auga one syllable or two?
Is the u in farum part of a diphthong?
items.answer: No. The a and u are in separate syllables: fa-rum.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark complete when you can pronounce all three main diphthongs correctly in ten random words.
